title: L'Alfabeto e la Pronuncia
subtitle: Italian spelling is famously regular — learn the handful of rules that make it so.
objectives: Say the 21 letters of the Italian alphabet
Pronounce c/g before different vowels correctly
Recognize gn, gl and sc as single sounds

content.intro: Italian is written almost exactly as it sounds. Once you know a small set of spelling rules, you can read any Italian word aloud correctly — even one you've never seen.
content.explanation:
The Italian alphabet has 21 native letters (no j, k, w, x, y — these appear only in loanwords like jeans or whisky). Every vowel (a, e, i, o, u) is always pronounced clearly and the same way — Italian has no silent vowels and no vowel reduction like English “the” becoming “thuh”.

The trickiest part for English speakers is that c and g change sound depending on the letter that follows them, and a few two/three-letter combinations represent a single sound.

rules.heading: a) C and G before vowels
rules.body:
• ca, co, cu = hard "k" sound — casa, cosa, cubo
  • ce, ci = soft "ch" sound (like English "cheese") — cena, cinema
  • ga, go, gu = hard "g" sound — gatto, gonna, guanto
  • ge, gi = soft "j" sound (like English "jet") — gelato, giorno

rules.heading: b) Keeping the hard/soft sound before e or i
rules.body:
• Add an h to keep the hard sound before e/i: che, chi = "k" (chi, "who"); ghe, ghi = hard "g" (spaghetti)
  • Add an i to keep the soft sound before a/o/u: cia, cio, ciu = "ch" (ciao); gia, gio, giu = "j" (giorno) — the i is silent here, just a spelling signal

rules.heading: c) Special combinations
rules.body:
• gn = "ny" as in canyon — gnocchi, bagno
  • gli = "ly" as in million — famiglia, figlio
  • sc before e/i = "sh" — pesce, sciare; before a/o/u = "sk" — scuola, pesca
  • Double consonants are held longer than single ones — sono (I am) vs. sonno (sleep) are genuinely different words

examples.en: Hi, what's your name? — ciao starts with the soft "ch" sound
I'm hungry, I want pasta — voglio has a soft "ly"-like gli is not here, but voglio's gli combo shows the pattern in famiglia
The cat sleeps on the bed — gatto has the hard "g" sound
My daughter studies at university — figlia uses the gli "ly" sound
The spaghetti is delicious — spaghetti keeps the hard "g" thanks to the h

commonMistakes.why: ci before a vowel is always the soft "ch" sound in Italian, unlike the hard c English speakers expect.

commonMistakes.wrong: Treating "sono" and "sonno" as the same word
commonMistakes.right: sono (I am / they are) vs. sonno (sleep, drowsiness) — genuinely different
commonMistakes.why: Double consonants change the meaning of the word, not just the spelling — they must be held longer in speech.

items.explanation: Ce/ci is always the soft "ch" sound in Italian.
gn is always a single "ny" sound, never two separate letters.

items.prompt: Which word has the hard "g" sound?
items.explanation: Ga/go/gu is hard; ge/gi is soft — gatto has ga, the hard sound.

exercises.title: Match the Spelling to Its Sound

items.explanation: The h and i in these combinations are silent spelling signals, not pronounced letters of their own.

summary: Every Italian vowel is pronounced clearly — there is no vowel reduction.
C/g are hard before a, o, u and soft before e, i; h keeps them hard, i keeps them soft.
gn = "ny", gli = "ly", sc(e/i) = "sh" — and double consonants are genuinely held longer.
